course.title: Sinhala Course
course.principle: Structured drills prepare the brain; unstructured video makes the language feel alive.

sentencePatterns.title: Sinhala usually saves the verb for the end
sentencePatterns.explanation: In many Sinhala story sentences, the actor comes early and the main action lands late. Train yourself to wait for the final verb before deciding what happened.

sentencePatterns.title: Sinhala uses endings where English uses prepositions
sentencePatterns.explanation: English says to me, from home, or with mother. Sinhala often attaches that job to the noun: මට, ගෙදරින්, අම්මත් එක්ක.

sentencePatterns.title: Negation comes after the idea being negated
sentencePatterns.explanation: Watch for නැහැ, නෑ, or බෑ near the end. It can flip the meaning after you have already heard most of the sentence.
sentencePatterns.exampleSi: මට විශ්වාසයි මේකේ කවුරුත් ජීවත් වෙන්නේ නැහැ.
sentencePatterns.exampleEn: I’m sure no one lives here.

sentencePatterns.title: ඕනේ carries want or need
sentencePatterns.explanation: Sinhala often frames wanting as something being needed to someone. The person may appear with -ට, as in මට or එයාට.
sentencePatterns.exampleSi: එයාට ආශාව ඉෂ්ට කරගන්න ඕනේ වුණා.
sentencePatterns.exampleEn: He/she wanted to fulfill the wish.

sentencePatterns.title: කියලා packages thoughts and speech
sentencePatterns.explanation: කියලා can mean that/said/thinking that. It is a signal that a whole idea has been bundled inside the sentence.
sentencePatterns.exampleSi: ඔහු තේරුම් ගත්තා වැරැද්දක් තියෙනවා කියලා.
sentencePatterns.exampleEn: He understood that something was wrong.

sentencePatterns.title: Connectors carry story logic
sentencePatterns.explanation: Words like ඉතින්, ඒත්, ඊට පස්සේ, හැබැයි, and ඒ නිසා tell you whether the story is continuing, contrasting, or giving a reason.
sentencePatterns.exampleSi: ඊට පස්සේ ඔහු ළඟා වුණා පරණ නිවසකට.
sentencePatterns.exampleEn: After that, he reached an old house.

scriptGrammarRules.title: Sinhala usually saves the verb for the end
scriptGrammarRules.explanation: In many Sinhala story sentences, the actor comes early and the main action lands late. Train yourself to wait for the final verb before deciding what happened.

scriptGrammarRules.title: Sinhala uses endings where English uses prepositions
scriptGrammarRules.explanation: English says to me, from home, or with mother. Sinhala often attaches that job to the noun: මට, ගෙදරින්, අම්මත් එක්ක.

scriptGrammarRules.title: Negation comes after the idea being negated
scriptGrammarRules.explanation: Watch for නැහැ, නෑ, or බෑ near the end. It can flip the meaning after you have already heard most of the sentence.

scriptGrammarRules.title: ඕනේ carries want or need
scriptGrammarRules.explanation: Sinhala often frames wanting as something being needed to someone. The person may appear with -ට, as in මට or එයාට.

scriptGrammarRules.title: කියලා packages thoughts and speech
scriptGrammarRules.explanation: කියලා can mean that/said/thinking that. It is a signal that a whole idea has been bundled inside the sentence.

scriptGrammarRules.title: Connectors carry story logic
scriptGrammarRules.explanation: Words like ඉතින්, ඒත්, ඊට පස්සේ, හැබැයි, and ඒ නිසා tell you whether the story is continuing, contrasting, or giving a reason.

scriptGrammarRules.title: Past events
scriptGrammarRules.explanation: Notice story verbs such as වුනා, ගියා, කළා, දැක්කා, and හිතුවා.

scriptGrammarRules.title: Negation
scriptGrammarRules.explanation: Sinhala commonly uses නැහැ or බෑ after the verb idea.

scriptGrammarRules.title: Needs and wants
scriptGrammarRules.explanation: ඕනේ marks wanting or needing; කැමති and ආසයි mark liking.

scriptGrammarRules.title: Case markers
scriptGrammarRules.explanation: Watch endings like -ට, -ගේ, and -ව for to/for, possession, and object marking.

scriptGrammarRules.title: Verb chains
scriptGrammarRules.explanation: Forms ending in -න්න often act like to do: යන්න, ගන්න, කරන්න.

grammarStructures.title: Default subject-object-verb order
grammarStructures.explanation: A neutral Sinhala sentence normally places the main verb last.

examples.en: I read the book.
I drink tea.
She writes a letter.
I drink coffee.
We listen to songs.
You make food.
He or she opens the door.
She starts the class.
They hit the ball.

grammarStructures.title: Time and place before the verb
grammarStructures.explanation: Time and place information usually arrives before the final action.

examples.en: I am going home today.
We are going to school tomorrow.
He or she goes to the shop in the morning.
I am going to the shop today.
We are going to the beach tomorrow.
He or she is staying home tonight.
She goes to the office in the morning.
They go to the temple in the evening.
You are going to class now.

grammarStructures.title: Omitted subjects
grammarStructures.explanation: Speakers often omit I, you, or they when context already makes the subject clear.

examples.en: I am going home now.
I will come tomorrow.
I will stay here for a little while.
I am going to the shop now.
I am coming again tomorrow.
I will stay a little.
I will talk later.
I am working today.
I will read slowly.

grammarStructures.title: Noun descriptions without 'is'
grammarStructures.explanation: Spoken Sinhala often joins two noun ideas without a separate present-tense word for 'is'.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: He or she is a teacher.

examples.en: He or she is a teacher.
She is a doctor.
I am a student.
He is a teacher.
She is a nurse.
I am a student.
We are friends.
He or she is a driver.
You are a traveler.

grammarStructures.title: Adjective descriptions
grammarStructures.explanation: Many descriptions work as complete predicates without an extra copula.

examples.en: This food is tasty.
The weather is good today.
That room is big.
This tea is tasty.
Today is quiet.
That story is long.
The air here is cool.
This road is empty.
That class is easy.

grammarStructures.title: There is with තියෙනවා
grammarStructures.explanation: Use තියෙනවා for the existence or location of many inanimate things.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: There is a book on the table.

examples.en: There is a book on the table.
There is water at home.
There is a key in the bag.
There is a bag under the table.
There is a new fan at home.
There is a chair near the window.
There are three cups in the cupboard.
There is a map in the classroom.
There is a pen inside the bag.

grammarStructures.title: People and animals with ඉන්නවා
grammarStructures.explanation: Use ඉන්නවා for where an animate being is or remains.

examples.en: Mother is at home.
The dog is in the yard.
The children are at school.
Father is at home.
The cat is in the kitchen.
The friends are outside.
The teacher is in the classroom.
Older sister is at the office.
The dog is by the door.

grammarStructures.title: This and that
grammarStructures.explanation: මේ points to something near the speaker; ඒ points to something already known or farther away.

examples.en: This book is mine.
That car is new.
This cup is yours.

grammarStructures.title: Yes-no questions with -ද
grammarStructures.explanation: A spoken statement can become a yes-no question by adding the question sound -ද.

examples.en: Are you coming today?
Is this correct?
Did you eat?
Are you leaving now?
Is this tea hot?
Is he or she coming tomorrow?
Are we staying here?
Is this yours?
Did they speak?

grammarStructures.title: Question words stay inside the sentence
grammarStructures.explanation: Words such as කවුද, මොකක්ද, කොහෙද, කවදාද, ඇයි, and කොහොමද normally remain where their answer would appear.

examples.en: Where are you going?
What are you eating?
When is he or she coming?
Who are you going with?
Where is he or she staying?
When are we leaving?
Why are you laughing?
How does this work?
Why did they come?

grammarStructures.title: Dative -ට for to, for, and experiencers
grammarStructures.explanation: The -ට ending can mark a recipient, destination, or the person who feels, needs, or experiences something.

examples.en: I need water.
She feels cold.
We do not have time.
I need more time.
Do you understand?
She is afraid.
We are free today.
He or she is happy.
They need help.

grammarStructures.title: Possession with -ගේ
grammarStructures.explanation: Attach -ගේ to an animate owner or pronoun to express possession.

examples.en: This is Nadee's book.
That is my friend's car.
This is the child's bag.
This is our house.
That is your phone.
This book is the teacher's.
Her cup is on the table.
Their car is parked.
This bag is my friend's.

grammarStructures.title: Animate objects with -ව
grammarStructures.explanation: A definite person or animal used as an object is often marked with -ව in colloquial Sinhala.

examples.en: I saw him or her.
She caught the dog.
We met the teacher.

grammarStructures.title: By or with using -න් / -ින්
grammarStructures.explanation: Instrumental forms can express the tool, means, or source involved in an event.

examples.en: I came by bus.
He or she wrote with a pencil.
We went to Kandy by train.

grammarStructures.title: From a place with -ින්
grammarStructures.explanation: The same family of endings commonly marks movement from a place.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: He or she left from home.

examples.en: He or she left from home.
I came from Colombo.
The bus left from Kandy.

grammarStructures.title: Together with using එක්ක
grammarStructures.explanation: Put එක්ක after a person or thing to mean with or together with.

examples.en: I went with my friend.
She spoke with Mother.
We played with the children.

grammarStructures.title: Relational location words
grammarStructures.explanation: Sinhala places location words after the noun they relate to.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: There is a shop near the school.

examples.en: There is a shop near the school.
The cat is under the chair.
There is a garden behind the house.
The phone is on the table.
The shoes are by the door.
It is cool inside the house.

examples.si: කාර් එක පිටිපස්සේ බෑග් එක තියෙනවා.
examples.en: The bag is behind the car.
The dog is in front of the chair.
The books are under the window.

grammarStructures.title: Present and regular actions with -නවා
grammarStructures.explanation: The common colloquial -නවා form covers present, habitual, and contextually future actions.

examples.en: I study Sinhala every day.
He or she drinks coffee in the morning.
We play cricket on weekends.
I drink water in the morning.
You work on Saturdays.
He or she walks in the evening.
We listen to Sinhala every day.
She cooks twice a week.
They play after school.

grammarStructures.title: Completed past events
grammarStructures.pattern: past verb form at the end
grammarStructures.explanation: Past forms vary by verb, so learn frequent forms such as ගියා, ආවා, කළා, දැක්කා, and කිව්වා as whole units.

examples.en: We went to Colombo yesterday.
She made breakfast.
I spoke to him yesterday.
I woke up early this morning.
You read well yesterday.
He or she came by bus.
We ate dinner at night.
She wrote a letter to her friend.
They arrived on time.

grammarStructures.title: Future meaning from time and context
grammarStructures.explanation: Colloquial Sinhala often uses a nonpast form with හෙට or another future time expression.

examples.en: I will come tomorrow.
We will go to Jaffna next week.
He or she will call tonight.
I will call tomorrow.
We will take a trip next month.
He or she will study tonight.
You will tell me later.
They have a meeting on Monday.
She will go home at the weekend.

grammarStructures.title: Negative actions with නැහැ / නෑ
grammarStructures.explanation: The negative particle follows the verbal idea and often changes the verb to a focused form.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: I am not going to work today.

examples.en: I am not going to work today.
She does not eat meat.
We are not going out today.
I do not forget this.

examples.si: ඔයා අද බස් එක ගන්නේ නෑ.
examples.en: You are not taking the bus today.
He or she is not there.
We do not know about this.
She does not drink coffee at night.
They are not going to be late.

grammarStructures.title: Direct requests and commands
grammarStructures.explanation: Short spoken commands often use a compact verb form; tone and politeness matter.

examples.en: Sit here.
Close the door.
Speak a little slowly.
Look here.
Bring the book.
Do not talk now.
Please hurry a little.
Do not forget that.
Go forward.

grammarStructures.title: Infinitives ending in -න්න
grammarStructures.explanation: The -න්න form expresses to do and combines with wants, ability, purpose, and other verbs.

examples.en: I want to speak Sinhala.
We need to leave early.
She went to the shop to buy the book.
I want to stay a little longer.
We need to understand this.
He or she went to the shop to buy bread.
She tried to fall asleep quickly.

examples.si: ඔවුන් ගමන පටන් ගන්න ලෑස්ති වුණා.
examples.en: They got ready to start the trip.
Can you read this?

grammarStructures.title: Chaining actions with -ලා
grammarStructures.explanation: A -ලා participle connects a completed action to the next event.

examples.en: I ate and went home.
He or she opened the door and went inside.

examples.si: මම තේ හදලා වැඩ පටන් ගත්තා.
examples.en: I made tea and started work.
I washed my hands and ate.

examples.si: එයා බෑග් එක අරගෙන පිටත් වුණා.
examples.en: He or she took the bag and left.
We closed the door and slept.

examples.si: ඇය කවුළුව ඇරලා පිට බලලා හිටියා.
examples.en: She opened the window and looked outside.
They made tea and invited us.
Read this and tell me.

grammarStructures.title: Irregular participles in event chains
grammarStructures.explanation: Frequent verbs have common chained forms worth learning as chunks.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: He or she went to the shop and bought bread.

examples.en: He or she went to the shop and bought bread.
We went to the market and bought vegetables.
She went home and slept.

grammarStructures.title: Speech and thought with කියලා
grammarStructures.explanation: කියලා packages words, thoughts, names, and propositions inside a larger sentence.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: He or she said that they are coming tomorrow.

examples.en: He or she said that they are coming tomorrow.
Mother said that the food is ready.

examples.si: මම ඒක හොඳ අදහසක් කියලා හිතනවා.
examples.en: I think that is a good idea.
He or she said that they would be late.
I thought this was easy.

examples.si: අපි හෙට එනවා කියලා දැනුම් දුන්නා.
examples.en: We informed them that we are coming tomorrow.

examples.si: ඇය ඔයාට කතා කරන්න කියලා මට කිව්වා.
examples.en: She told me to speak to you.
They think it is going to rain.

examples.si: මට එයා එතන ඉන්නවා කියලා ආරංචි වුණා.
examples.en: I heard that he or she is there.

grammarStructures.title: Reasons with නිසා
grammarStructures.explanation: The reason normally comes first, followed by නිසා and then the result.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: Because of the rain, we did not go.

examples.en: Because of the rain, we did not go.

examples.si: රථවාහන තදබදය නිසා එයා පරක්කු වුණා.
examples.en: He or she was late because of traffic.

examples.si: විදුලිය නැති නිසා වැඩ නතර වුණා.
examples.en: The work stopped because there was no electricity.

examples.si: කාලය නැති නිසා අපි ඉක්මන් කළා.
examples.en: We hurried because there was no time.

examples.si: සද්දෙ වැඩි නිසා මට අහන්න බැරි වුණා.
examples.en: I could not hear because the noise was loud.

examples.si: අද සිසිල නිසා එයා ජැකට් එක ඇන්දා.
examples.en: He or she wore a jacket because it was cool today.

examples.si: වැඩ වැඩි නිසා ඇය පරක්කු වුණා.
examples.en: She was late because there was a lot of work.

examples.si: බස් නැති නිසා ඔවුන් ඇවිදගෙන ගියා.
examples.en: They walked because there was no bus.

examples.si: ඔයා කතා කළ නිසා මට තේරුණා.
examples.en: I understood because you explained it.

grammarStructures.title: Colloquial reasons with හින්දා
grammarStructures.explanation: හින්දා is a very common conversational way to introduce the cause of a result.
grammarStructures.exampleSi: මට වැඩ තිබුණ හින්දා එන්න බැරි වුණා.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: I could not come because I had work.

examples.si: මට වැඩ තිබුණ හින්දා එන්න බැරි වුණා.
examples.en: I could not come because I had work.

examples.si: වැස්ස වැඩි හින්දා අපි ඇතුළේ හිටියා.
examples.en: We stayed inside because it was raining heavily.

examples.si: මට සනීප නැති හින්දා වැඩට ගියේ නැහැ.
examples.en: I did not go to work because I was unwell.

grammarStructures.title: When clauses with කොට / වෙලාවේ
grammarStructures.explanation: A time-setting clause normally comes before the main event.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: When I come home, Mother is cooking.

examples.en: When I come home, Mother is cooking.
When he or she comes, we will be eating.

examples.si: මම කඩේට යනකොට වැස්ස පටන් ගත්තා.
examples.en: When I was going to the shop, it started raining.

grammarStructures.title: Until with කන්
grammarStructures.explanation: කන් marks the endpoint up to which another situation continues.

examples.en: Stay here until I come.
We waited until the rain stopped.

examples.si: වැඩ ඉවර වෙනකන් එයා ගියේ නැහැ.
examples.en: He or she did not leave until the work was finished.

grammarStructures.title: Conditions with නම්
grammarStructures.explanation: නම් can mark if or as for, depending on whether it frames a condition or a topic.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: If you are coming, tell me.

examples.en: If you are coming, tell me.

examples.si: වෙලාව තියෙනවා නම් අපි හම්බ වෙමු.
examples.en: If there is time, let us meet.

examples.si: මේක අමාරු නම් මම උදව් කරන්නම්.
examples.en: If this is difficult, I will help.
If there is water, give me some.
If you are ready, let us go.
If this is correct, sign it.
If he or she has time, they will come.
If it does not rain, we will stay outside.
If they want, they will join.

grammarStructures.title: Compact conditions with -ොත්
grammarStructures.explanation: The suffixed -ොත් form creates a compact if-clause.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: If it rains, let us stay home.

examples.en: If it rains, let us stay home.
If you come, let us go together.
If he or she calls, tell me.

grammarStructures.title: Even if and although
grammarStructures.explanation: These forms concede one fact before giving a result that still holds.

examples.en: Although it rained, we went.
Although it was difficult, she tried.

examples.si: පරක්කු වුණත් අපි වැඩේ ඉවර කළා.
examples.en: Even though it was late, we finished the work.

grammarStructures.title: Clauses that describe nouns
grammarStructures.explanation: A verb-based description comes before the noun it modifies.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: The man who came yesterday is my friend.

examples.en: The man who came yesterday is my friend.
The book that is on the table is mine.
The film that we watched yesterday is good.

grammarStructures.title: Wants and needs with ඕනේ
grammarStructures.explanation: The person who wants something often appears in the dative form.

examples.en: I want a tea.
I want a bottle of water.
We need two rooms.

grammarStructures.title: Ability with පුළුවන්
grammarStructures.explanation: The person able to act normally takes -ට; put the action in the -න්න form before පුළුවන්.
grammarStructures.exampleSi: මට ටිකක් සිංහල කතා කරන්න පුළුවන්.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: I can speak a little Sinhala.

examples.si: මට ටිකක් සිංහල කතා කරන්න පුළුවන්.
examples.en: I can speak a little Sinhala.
She can cook well.
Can you read this?
I can read a little Sinhala.
Can you lift this?
He or she can run fast.
We can come tomorrow.

examples.si: ඇයට ඒ ගීය ගායනා කරන්න පුළුවන්.
examples.en: She can sing that song.
They can find the way.

grammarStructures.title: Inability with බෑ
grammarStructures.explanation: බෑ expresses cannot, inability, or refusal in a compact spoken form.

examples.en: I cannot come today.
I cannot understand that.
We cannot stop now.

grammarStructures.title: Likes with කැමතියි and ආසයි
grammarStructures.explanation: The person who likes something commonly takes a dative form such as මට.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: I like listening to Sinhala songs.

examples.en: I like listening to Sinhala songs.
She likes looking at the sea.

examples.si: අපිට අලුත් කෑම රස බලන්න ආසයි.
examples.en: We like trying new food.
I like drinking hot tea.
Do you like this song?
He or she likes listening to the rain.
We like staying near the sea.

examples.si: ඇය අලුත් වචන ඉගෙන ගන්න ආසයි.
examples.en: She likes learning new words.
They like walking on Saturdays.

grammarStructures.title: Polite requests with පුළුවන්ද
grammarStructures.explanation: Ask whether an action is possible to soften a request.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: Could you explain this a little?

examples.en: Could you explain this a little?
Could you open the window?
Could you tell me the way?
Could you give me a little water?
Could you say this word again?
Could you open the door a little?
Could you write this down for me?
Could you come quickly?
Could you explain that to me?

grammarStructures.title: Asking permission
grammarStructures.explanation: Permission questions often use a question ending or ask whether doing the action is possible.

examples.en: May I sit here?
May I come in?
May I look at this?

grammarStructures.title: Obligation and necessity
grammarStructures.explanation: Use ඕනේ for need or must and වෙනවා for something that has to happen.

examples.en: I have to go now.

examples.si: අපිට අද මේක ඉවර කරන්න වෙනවා.
examples.en: We have to finish this today.
She has to wake up early.

examples.si: මට අද මේක ඉවර කරන්න වෙනවා.
examples.en: I have to finish this today.
You have to leave very early.
He or she has to meet the doctor.
We have to bring the documents.
She has to call again.
They have to decide today.

grammarStructures.title: Let's with -මු
grammarStructures.explanation: The hortative ending invites the listener to do something together.

examples.en: Let us eat.
Let us go now.
Let us rest for a while.

grammarStructures.title: Do not with එපා
grammarStructures.explanation: එපා follows an action to prohibit it and can also mean not wanted.

examples.en: Do not be afraid.
Do not smoke here.
Do not touch that.

grammarStructures.title: Confirmation with නේද
grammarStructures.explanation: නේද asks the listener to confirm something the speaker expects to be true.

examples.en: You are coming tomorrow, right?
This is yours, right?
We are meeting tomorrow, right?
You are coming today, right?
This road is right, isn't it?
He or she understands this, right?
We are talking later, right?
That bag is yours, right?
There is class tomorrow, right?

grammarStructures.title: Emphasis with තමයි
grammarStructures.explanation: තමයි highlights the person, time, place, or fact that answers the central question.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: I am the one who did it.

examples.en: I am the one who did it.
He or she is the one who helped me.
Today is when we are leaving.

grammarStructures.title: Managing a conversation with connectors
grammarStructures.explanation: These words continue, redirect, contrast, or advance a conversation.

examples.en: But I have another question.
So, what happened after that?
But I do not agree with that.

grammarStructures.title: Completed relevance with -ලා තියෙනවා
grammarStructures.explanation: This construction presents a completed action as relevant to the current situation.

examples.en: I have read that book.
She has been to Sri Lanka.
We have watched that film.

grammarStructures.title: Ongoing action with -මින් ඉන්නවා
grammarStructures.explanation: This more explicit progressive highlights an action continuing over time.

examples.en: He or she is working.
The children are playing.
I am writing the report.

grammarStructures.title: Voluntary and involuntary events
grammarStructures.pattern: agentive action vs experiencer + involuntary event
grammarStructures.explanation: Sinhala can mark whether an event was controlled or happened unintentionally, often changing both verb form and subject case.

examples.en: I forgot it unintentionally.
I accidentally broke the cup.
He or she accidentally missed the bus.

grammarStructures.title: Causing someone to act
grammarStructures.explanation: Causative forms express making, having, or causing another participant to do something.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: The teacher has the children write sentences.

examples.en: The teacher has the children write sentences.
Mother makes the child drink the medicine.
The coach makes the players run.

grammarStructures.title: Doing a favor with -ලා දෙනවා
grammarStructures.explanation: Adding දෙනවා can frame an action as being done for someone else.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: I will write that for you.

examples.en: I will write that for you.
She made food for me.
I will show you the way.

grammarStructures.title: Doing something for oneself with -ලා ගන්නවා
grammarStructures.explanation: Adding ගන්නවා can show that the subject obtains or completes something for their own benefit.

examples.en: I made myself a tea.
He or she chose a new shirt for themself.
I kept some food for myself.

grammarStructures.title: Passive and event-centered clauses
grammarStructures.explanation: Passive-like forms background the actor and foreground what happened to the affected participant.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: This work will be done tomorrow.

examples.en: This work will be done tomorrow.
The letter will be sent today.
These houses are being built anew.

grammarStructures.title: Focused verb forms
grammarStructures.explanation: Questions, negation, and emphasis often trigger a focused form of the verb rather than the neutral declarative form.

examples.en: Where did you go?
What did you buy?
When did he or she come?

grammarStructures.title: Topic-comment organization
grammarStructures.explanation: A topic can be established first, followed by what the speaker wants to say about it.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: As for this book, it is very interesting.

examples.en: As for this book, it is very interesting.
As for today, it is very hot.
As for that shop, the food is good.

grammarStructures.title: Flexible order for information focus
grammarStructures.pattern: arguments may move; discourse controls emphasis
grammarStructures.explanation: Sinhala is verb-final by default, but speakers move constituents to foreground contrast, topic, or new information.
grammarStructures.exampleSi: ඒ පොත මම ඊයේ තමයි ගත්තේ.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: That book, I bought only yesterday.

examples.si: ඒ පොත මම ඊයේ තමයි ගත්තේ.
examples.en: That book, I bought only yesterday.
It was yesterday that we went to Colombo.
I am not the one who did that.

grammarStructures.title: Comparisons with වඩා
grammarStructures.explanation: The comparison standard is followed by වඩා before the quality being compared.

examples.en: This is easier than that.
The train is faster than the bus.
Today is colder than yesterday.

examples.si: මේ ගමන ඊයේ ගමනට වඩා දිගයි.
examples.en: This trip is longer than yesterday's trip.
Coffee is stronger than tea.

examples.si: අද පාර කල්පනා කළාට වඩා හිස්.
examples.en: The road is emptier today than I expected.

examples.si: මේ කාමරය අනිත් එකට වඩා සිසිලයි.
examples.en: This room is cooler than the other one.

examples.si: එයාට වඩා ඇය හෙමින් කතා කරනවා.
examples.en: She speaks more slowly than he does.
The train is faster than the bus.

grammarStructures.title: Strongest degree with වඩාත්ම
grammarStructures.explanation: වඩාත්ම highlights the greatest degree of a quality.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: This is the most important part.

examples.en: This is the most important part.
She is the most capable student in the class.
This is our biggest problem.

grammarStructures.title: Embedding a question
grammarStructures.explanation: Question content can be packaged with කියලා inside a larger clause.
grammarStructures.exampleSi: එයා කවදා එයිද කියලා මම දන්නේ නැහැ.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: I do not know when he or she will come.

examples.si: එයා කවදා එයිද කියලා මම දන්නේ නැහැ.
examples.en: I do not know when he or she will come.

examples.si: බස් එක කොහෙද නවත්වන්නේ කියලා මම ඇහුවා.
examples.en: I asked where the bus stops.

examples.si: එයා ඇයි ගියේ කියලා අපි දන්නේ නැහැ.
examples.en: We do not know why he or she left.

examples.si: එයා කවදාද එන්නේ කියලා මම ඇහුවා.
examples.en: I asked when he or she is coming.
Ask what this is.

examples.si: අපි කොහෙද හම්බ වෙන්නේ කියලා තීරණය කළා.
examples.en: We decided where we are meeting.

examples.si: ඔවුන් ඇයි පරක්කු වුණේ කියලා කතා කළා.
examples.en: They discussed why they were late.

examples.si: මට ඇය මොනවද ගත්තේ කියලා දැනගන්න ඕනේ.
examples.en: I want to know what she bought.

examples.si: බස් එක කීයටද යන්නේ කියලා ඔහු ඇහුවා.
examples.en: He asked what time the bus leaves.

grammarStructures.title: Spoken and formal register choices
grammarStructures.explanation: Sinhala is diglossic. Daily conversation and formal writing often use different pronouns, verb endings, and vocabulary.

examples.en: Where are you going? (colloquial)
How are you? (formal)
How are you? (colloquial)

grammarStructures.title: Indefinite singular nouns with -ක් / -ෙක්
grammarStructures.explanation: A singular noun meaning a or one commonly carries an indefinite ending. The exact form depends on the noun and whether it is animate.

examples.en: I have a book.
There is a dog outside.
She got a tea.

grammarStructures.title: Plural nouns use several patterns
grammarStructures.explanation: Sinhala has several plural patterns rather than one universal ending, so learn frequent nouns together with their plurals.

examples.en: The children are at school.
There are books on the table.
People are waiting for the bus.

grammarStructures.title: Colloquial personal pronouns
grammarStructures.explanation: Everyday spoken Sinhala distinguishes singular and plural pronouns, while ඔබ is a more formal or respectful you.

examples.en: Where are you all going?
We are learning Sinhala.
They are working today.

grammarStructures.title: Possessive pronouns with -ගේ
grammarStructures.explanation: Common possessors include මගේ, ඔයාගේ, එයාගේ, අපේ, and ඔයාලාගේ.

examples.en: This is my bag.
Is that your book?
Our house is here.

grammarStructures.title: Adjectives come before nouns
grammarStructures.explanation: A descriptive adjective normally appears before the noun and does not change for gender or number in ordinary spoken Sinhala.

examples.en: I want the red shirt.
That is a big house.
These are new books.

grammarStructures.title: Joining nouns with -යි ... -යි
grammarStructures.explanation: In speech, -යි can mark each item in a coordinated list. සහ is a more formal alternative for and.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: Mother and father are at home.

examples.en: Mother and father are at home.
There is both tea and coffee.
Nimal and Kamal are coming tomorrow.

grammarStructures.title: Also and too with -ත්
grammarStructures.explanation: The particle -ත් adds the meaning also, too, or even to the item before it.

examples.en: I am coming tomorrow too.
He or she wants tea too.
We speak Sinhala too.

grammarStructures.title: Here, there, and over there
grammarStructures.explanation: මෙතන points near the speaker, එතන points to a known or addressee-side place, and අතන points farther away.

examples.en: The book is here.
You stay there.
The bus stop is over there.

grammarStructures.title: Having with a dative possessor
grammarStructures.explanation: Spoken Sinhala often expresses have as something existing to a person. Use ඉන්නවා when the possessed referent is animate.

examples.en: I have a car.
He or she has a brother.
We have time today.

grammarStructures.title: Feelings and bodily states with -ට
grammarStructures.explanation: Hunger, thirst, cold, sleepiness, and many feelings are framed as states experienced by someone.

examples.en: I am hungry.
She feels cold.
We are sleepy.

grammarStructures.title: Experiencers with මට, ඔයාට, and එයාට
grammarStructures.explanation: For wants, needs, ability, liking, feelings, and many bodily states, everyday Sinhala commonly marks the person with -ට. Do not automatically copy an English subject pronoun into Sinhala.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: I want or need to eat.

examples.en: I want or need to eat.
You can do this.
He or she needs help.
I like drinking hot tea.
Do you like listening to this song?
I am hungry today.
He or she feels cold.

grammarStructures.title: Recipients and destinations with -ට
grammarStructures.explanation: -ට can mark the person who receives something or the place someone moves toward. It does not make that word a direct object.

examples.en: I gave Mom a book.
I sent you a message.
I am going to the hospital.
He or she gave Mom a tea.
We are going to the shop.
I will show you the way.
He or she went home.

grammarStructures.title: Pronoun direct objects with -ව
grammarStructures.explanation: Use forms such as මාව, ඔයාව, and එයාව when a person is directly affected by an action. Keep them separate from dative forms such as මට and ඔයාට.

examples.en: He or she saw me.
I saw you.
We met him or her.
Did you see us?
He or she knows you.
I met Mom.
He or she caught the dog.

grammarStructures.title: Numerals commonly follow the noun
grammarStructures.explanation: In a neutral quantity phrase, Sinhala commonly places the counted noun before its numeral.

examples.en: I have three books.
I bought two mangoes.
There are four chairs in the room.

grammarStructures.title: Ordinal numbers before nouns
grammarStructures.explanation: Ordinal forms such as first and second normally come before the noun they rank.

examples.en: This is the first lesson.
He or she took the second bus.
Today is the third day.

grammarStructures.title: Manner words before the action
grammarStructures.explanation: Words describing how an action happens, such as slowly or well, usually appear before the final verb.

examples.en: Please speak slowly.
He or she speaks Sinhala well.
The bus went quickly.

grammarStructures.title: About with ගැන
grammarStructures.explanation: The postposition ගැන follows the topic and means about or concerning.

examples.en: We talked about the movie.

examples.si: මේ පොත ගැන ඔයා මොකද හිතන්නේ?
examples.en: What do you think about this book?
The teacher spoke about the exam.

grammarStructures.title: Similarity with වගේ
grammarStructures.explanation: වගේ follows a noun or phrase to express like, similar to, or as if.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: He or she speaks like you.

examples.en: He or she speaks like you.
This is like a dream.
Her voice is like Mother's.

grammarStructures.title: Alternatives with හරි ... හරි
grammarStructures.explanation: Repeating හරි after alternatives creates an everyday either-or choice.

examples.en: Have either tea or coffee.
Come either today or tomorrow.

examples.si: බස් එකෙන් හරි දුම්රියෙන් හරි යමු.
examples.en: Let us go either by bus or by train.

grammarStructures.title: Before doing with කලින්
grammarStructures.explanation: Place කලින් after an infinitive to say before doing that action.

examples.en: Call me before you leave.
Wash your hands before eating.

examples.si: වැඩ පටන් ගන්න කලින් මේක කියවන්න.
examples.en: Read this before starting the work.

grammarStructures.title: After an event with පස්සේ
grammarStructures.explanation: පස්සේ follows an event expression to place the main event afterward.

examples.en: We left after eating.

examples.si: වැඩ ඉවර වුණාට පස්සේ මම ගෙදර ගියා.
examples.en: I went home after the work finished.

examples.si: එයා ආවට පස්සේ අපි කතා කළා.
examples.en: We talked after he or she arrived.

grammarStructures.title: Doing two things with -න ගමන්
grammarStructures.pattern: ongoing action + න ගමන් + main action
grammarStructures.explanation: The construction -න ගමන් links an action continuing in the background with another action.
grammarStructures.exampleSi: බස් එකේ යන ගමන් මම පොතක් කියෙව්වා.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: I read a book while riding the bus.

examples.si: බස් එකේ යන ගමන් මම පොතක් කියෙව්වා.
examples.en: I read a book while riding the bus.

examples.si: කෑම උයන ගමන් ඇය සින්දු ඇහුවා.
examples.en: She listened to songs while cooking.

examples.si: පාරේ යන ගමන් අපි කතා කළා.
examples.en: We talked while walking along the road.

grammarStructures.title: While or when with -ද්දී
grammarStructures.explanation: The spoken ending -ද්දී places one event during another event or situation.
grammarStructures.exampleSi: මම වැඩ කරද්දී එයා කතා කළා.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: He or she called while I was working.

examples.si: මම වැඩ කරද්දී එයා කතා කළා.
examples.en: He or she called while I was working.
He or she came while we were eating.
The children ran inside while it was raining.

grammarStructures.title: Trying an action with -ලා බලන්න
grammarStructures.explanation: After another verb, බලන්න can mean try doing it and see what happens.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: Try eating a little of this food.

examples.en: Try eating a little of this food.
Try saying this word.
Try writing it again.

grammarStructures.title: Finished actions with -ලා ඉවරයි
grammarStructures.explanation: This construction says that an action has been completed or is all done.

examples.en: I have finished the work.
He or she has finished eating.
We have finished writing the report.

grammarStructures.title: Beginning an action with පටන් ගන්නවා
grammarStructures.explanation: Place an infinitive before පටන් ගන්නවා to say that an action starts.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: It started raining in the evening.

examples.en: It started raining in the evening.
The child started crying.

examples.si: අපි උදේ වැඩ කරන්න පටන් ගත්තා.
examples.en: We started working in the morning.

grammarStructures.title: Formal that-clauses with බව
grammarStructures.explanation: බව packages a fact as a noun-like clause, especially in formal speech and writing; colloquial speech often prefers කියලා.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: I know that he is coming.

examples.en: I know that he is coming.

examples.si: රැස්වීම අවලංගු කළ බව ඔවුන් දැනුම් දුන්නා.
examples.en: They announced that the meeting was canceled.
It appears that this information is correct.

grammarStructures.title: Someone or something with question word + හරි
grammarStructures.explanation: A question word followed by හරි creates an indefinite expression such as someone, something, or somewhere.

examples.en: Someone is at the door.
I want something to eat.
Let us go somewhere.

grammarStructures.title: Nobody and nothing with -ත්/-වත් plus negation
grammarStructures.explanation: With a negative predicate, forms such as කවුරුත් and මොනවත් mean nobody and nothing.

examples.en: Nobody came.
I did not eat anything.
He or she did not go anywhere.

grammarStructures.title: Only with විතරයි
grammarStructures.explanation: විතරයි follows the limited item and means only or just that amount.

examples.en: I only have five minutes.
Only I am working today.
We only need to take these two.

grammarStructures.title: At least and even with -වත්
grammarStructures.explanation: Outside a negative expression, -වත් can set a minimum meaning at least or emphasize even.

examples.en: Try at least once.
Drink at least a little water.
Stay for at least ten minutes.

grammarStructures.title: Reported or hearsay information with ලු
grammarStructures.explanation: Sentence-final ලු signals that the speaker heard the information from someone else rather than asserting it directly.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: They say he or she is coming tomorrow.

examples.en: They say he or she is coming tomorrow.
They say the food at the new shop is good.
I heard that tomorrow is a holiday.

grammarStructures.title: Shared understanding with නේ
grammarStructures.explanation: Sentence-final නේ can invite agreement, remind the listener of shared knowledge, or mark a realization. Its force depends on intonation.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: It is really hot today, isn't it?

examples.en: It is really hot today, isn't it?
You know that, right.
This route is easy, isn't it?

grammarStructures.title: Probability and inference with ඇති
grammarStructures.explanation: Clause-final ඇති can present a conclusion as probable rather than certain.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: He or she is probably at home now.

examples.en: He or she is probably at home now.
The bus has probably been delayed.
They have probably already left.

grammarStructures.title: It seems or looks like with වගේ
grammarStructures.explanation: At the end of a situation description, වගේ marks an impression or appearance rather than a firm fact.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: It looks like it will rain today.

examples.en: It looks like it will rain today.
He or she seems tired.
This task seems difficult.

grammarStructures.title: Reflexive reference with තමන්
grammarStructures.explanation: තමන් refers back to the contextually relevant person and can mean oneself, himself, herself, or themselves.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: You also need to think about yourself.

examples.en: You also need to think about yourself.
He or she admitted their own mistake.

examples.si: හැමෝම තමන්ට පුළුවන් විදිහට උදව් කළා.
examples.en: Everyone helped in the way they could.

grammarStructures.title: Reciprocal actions with එකිනෙකා
grammarStructures.explanation: එකිනෙකා expresses each other and takes the ending required by its role in the sentence.

examples.en: We helped each other.
They looked at each other.
Let us listen to each other's ideas.

grammarStructures.title: Formal obligation with යුතුයි
grammarStructures.explanation: Formal instructions and writing often use යුතුයි for should or must, where conversation may prefer ඕනේ or වෙනවා.

examples.en: You must complete this application.

examples.si: සියලු දෙනා නියමිත වේලාවට පැමිණිය යුතුයි.
examples.en: Everyone must arrive at the appointed time.
These rules must be followed.

grammarStructures.title: Written copula වේ
grammarStructures.explanation: Formal written Sinhala can use වේ as is or becomes, while ordinary conversation often uses no separate copula.

examples.en: This is an important point.

examples.si: කොළඹ ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ ප්‍රධාන නගරය වේ.
examples.en: Colombo is the principal city of Sri Lanka.
Education is a fundamental right.

grammarStructures.title: Written future with -නු ඇත
grammarStructures.explanation: Formal forecasts and writing may mark future time with -නු ඇත; colloquial Sinhala usually relies on a nonpast form plus context.

examples.en: He will arrive tomorrow.

examples.si: වැඩසටහන ලබන සතියේ ආරම්භ වනු ඇත.
examples.en: The program will begin next week.
The results will be released tomorrow.

grammarStructures.title: Action nouns with -ීම
grammarStructures.explanation: The ending -ීම turns an action into a noun, especially in formal writing, headings, and instructions.

examples.en: Reading every day is important.
Smoking is prohibited.
Learning a language takes time.

grammarStructures.title: Time contrasts inside relative clauses
grammarStructures.pattern: nonpast or past describing verb + noun
grammarStructures.explanation: The verb before a noun shows whether the describing event is ongoing, expected, habitual, or completed.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: The man who came yesterday is my teacher.

examples.en: The man who came yesterday is my teacher.

examples.si: දැන් කතා කරන කෙනා මගේ යාළුවා.
examples.en: The person speaking now is my friend.

examples.si: හෙට එන අමුත්තන්ට කාමර දෙකක් ඕනේ.
examples.en: The guests coming tomorrow need two rooms.

grammarStructures.title: Repetition for gradual or repeated action
grammarStructures.explanation: Repeating a word or verb can express gradual change, distribution, continuation, or repeated action.
grammarStructures.exampleSi: මම ටික ටික සිංහල ඉගෙන ගන්නවා.
grammarStructures.exampleEn: I am learning Sinhala little by little.

examples.si: මම ටික ටික සිංහල ඉගෙන ගන්නවා.
examples.en: I am learning Sinhala little by little.
The children came inside one by one.

examples.si: එයා ඒ දිහා බලා බලා හිටියා.
examples.en: He or she kept looking at it.

conversations.title: Greeting someone
conversations.contextEn: You meet a friend in the morning.
conversations.replyEn: I am well. How are you?

variants.replyEn: I am well. How are you?

conversations.title: Introducing your name
conversations.contextEn: Someone asks your name.
conversations.replyEn: My name is Rehana.

variants.aEn: Can you tell me your name?
What name do people call you by?
Could you tell me your name?

conversations.title: Saying where you are from
conversations.contextEn: A new acquaintance asks where you are from.
conversations.replyEn: I am from America.

distractors.en: He or she is a teacher.

conversations.title: Talking about Sinhala ability
conversations.contextEn: Someone asks whether you speak Sinhala.
conversations.replyEn: I can speak a little.

distractors.en: He or she is not at home.

conversations.title: Thanks and acknowledgment
conversations.contextEn: Someone helps you.
conversations.replyEn: Thank you very much.

conversations.title: Ending a conversation
conversations.contextEn: You are leaving after a visit.
conversations.replyEn: Okay, travel safely.

conversations.title: Asking a price
conversations.contextEn: You are shopping at a market.
conversations.replyEn: This is five hundred rupees.

variants.aEn: How much are two of these?

variants.replyEn: It is one thousand five hundred rupees.

variants.aEn: How much are three of these?
variants.replyEn: All three are one thousand rupees.
I can reduce it a little.

conversations.title: Ordering food
conversations.contextEn: A server asks what you want.
conversations.replySi: මට බත් එකක් සහ වතුර ඕනේ.
conversations.replyEn: I would like rice and water.

variants.replySi: මට බත් එකක් සහ වතුර ඕනේ.
variants.replyEn: I would like rice and water.

variants.aEn: What would you like to drink?
What would you like to eat?
variants.replyEn: I would like a rice meal.

variants.aEn: What would you like to drink?
variants.replyEn: I would like a lemon juice.

variants.aEn: Would you like one more thing?
variants.replyEn: Yes, I would like a little sambol.

conversations.title: Asking for directions
conversations.contextEn: You need to find the railway station.
conversations.replyEn: Go straight and turn left.

variants.replyEn: It is ahead on the right.

variants.aEn: How do I get to the hospital?
How do I get to the bank?
Does this road go to the bus stop?
variants.replyEn: Yes, it is a little further ahead.

conversations.title: Taking a bus
conversations.contextEn: You are checking whether a bus goes to Kandy.
conversations.aEn: Does this bus go to Kandy?
conversations.replyEn: Yes, it goes to Kandy.

variants.aEn: Does this bus go to Kandy?
Does this train go to Colombo?
variants.replyEn: Yes, it leaves in ten minutes.

conversations.title: Asking the time
conversations.contextEn: You do not know the current time.
conversations.replyEn: It is three thirty now.

variants.aEn: What time does the bus come?
What time does the shop close?
variants.replyEn: It closes at eight in the evening.

conversations.title: Asking for help
conversations.contextEn: You cannot understand a form.
conversations.replyEn: Okay, I will help.

variants.replyEn: I will show you the way.

variants.aEn: I do not understand this word.
Could you read this letter for me?
variants.replyEn: Yes, I will read it for you.

conversations.title: Recounting yesterday
conversations.contextEn: A friend asks what you did yesterday.
conversations.replySi: මම යාළුවෙක් හම්බ වෙලා චිත්‍රපටයක් බැලුවා.
conversations.replyEn: I met a friend and watched a movie.

variants.replySi: මම යාළුවෙක් හම්බ වෙලා චිත්‍රපටයක් බැලුවා.
variants.replyEn: I met a friend and watched a movie.
There was a lot of work, but it was good.

variants.aEn: What did you do last night?
Who did you go with yesterday?

variants.replyEn: Yes, it was a good day.

conversations.title: Explaining why you were late
conversations.contextEn: Someone asks why you arrived late.
conversations.replySi: බස් එක පරක්කු වුණ හින්දා මමත් පරක්කු වුණා.
conversations.replyEn: I was late because the bus was late.

distractors.en: The book is on the table.

variants.replySi: බස් එක පරක්කු වුණ හින්දා මමත් පරක්කු වුණා.
variants.replyEn: I was late because the bus was late.

variants.aEn: Why did you not come to the meeting?
variants.replySi: මට සනීප නැති හින්දා එන්න බැරි වුණා.
variants.replyEn: I could not come because I was unwell.

variants.aEn: Why is the work not finished?
variants.replySi: විදුලිය නැති නිසා වැඩ නතර වුණා.
variants.replyEn: The work stopped because there was no electricity.

conversations.title: Describing a lost item
conversations.contextEn: You are looking for your phone.
conversations.replySi: මම ඊයේ ගත්ත කළු ෆෝන් එක හොයනවා.
conversations.replyEn: I am looking for the black phone I bought yesterday.

variants.replySi: මම ඊයේ ගත්ත කළු ෆෝන් එක හොයනවා.
variants.replyEn: I am looking for the black phone I bought yesterday.

variants.replySi: මම ඒක බස් එකේ දාලා ඇවිත් වගේ.
variants.replyEn: I think I left it on the bus.

variants.aEn: What does the bag look like?
variants.replyEn: It is a small blue bag.

conversations.title: Explaining a sequence
conversations.contextEn: A friend asks what happened next.
conversations.replyEn: He or she opened the door and went inside.

variants.replyEn: He or she opened the door and went inside.

variants.aEn: Where did you go after that?
variants.replyEn: After that we went to the shop.
First I went to the shop.

variants.replySi: ඊට පස්සේ අපි බස් එකට නැග්ගා.
variants.replyEn: After that we got on the bus.

variants.aEn: Where did you arrive in the end?
variants.replyEn: In the end we arrived home.

variants.aEn: So what did you do then?
variants.replyEn: Then I called him or her.

conversations.title: Making a conditional plan
conversations.contextEn: You are planning around the weather.
conversations.aEn: What will we do if it rains tomorrow?
conversations.replySi: වැස්සොත් අපි ගෙදර ඉඳලා චිත්‍රපටයක් බලමු.
conversations.replyEn: If it rains, let us stay home and watch a movie.

variants.aEn: What will we do if it rains tomorrow?
variants.replySi: වැස්සොත් අපි ගෙදර ඉඳලා චිත්‍රපටයක් බලමු.
variants.replyEn: If it rains, let us stay home and watch a movie.

variants.aEn: What will you do if there is time?
variants.replyEn: If there is time, I will read the book.

variants.aEn: How will you go if there is no bus?
variants.replyEn: If there is no bus, let us go by train.

conversations.title: Passing on a message
conversations.contextEn: A friend asks what Nadee said.
conversations.replyEn: She said that she is coming tomorrow.

variants.replyEn: She said that she is coming tomorrow.
She said the food is ready.
The teacher said there is a test tomorrow.

conversations.title: Asking for clarification
conversations.contextEn: Someone spoke too quickly.
conversations.replyEn: A little. Could you say it again slowly?

variants.replyEn: A little. Could you say it again slowly?
Could you say the last part again?

variants.aEn: Could you say that a little more slowly?
variants.replyEn: Yes, I will say it again.

variants.aEn: I do not understand this part.
variants.replyEn: Okay, I will explain with an example.

variants.aEn: What do you mean by this?
variants.replySi: මම කියන්නේ අපි දැන් යමු කියලා.
variants.replyEn: I mean that we should go now.

conversations.title: Accepting an invitation
conversations.contextEn: A friend invites you to dinner.
conversations.aSi: අද රෑ අපිත් එක්ක කෑම කන්න එනවද?
conversations.aEn: Will you come eat with us tonight?
conversations.replyEn: Yes, I would be happy to come.

variants.aSi: අද රෑ අපිත් එක්ක කෑම කන්න එනවද?
variants.aEn: Will you come eat with us tonight?
variants.replyEn: Yes, I would be happy to come.

variants.aEn: Shall we watch a film on Saturday?
Will you come for tea tomorrow?

conversations.title: Declining politely
conversations.contextEn: You cannot accept an invitation.
conversations.aEn: Can you come with us tomorrow?
conversations.replyEn: Sorry, I have work tomorrow.

variants.aEn: Can you come with us tomorrow?

conversations.title: Giving an opinion

referenceLessons.title: Family and people
referenceLessons.goal: Name close relatives and say who someone is.

grammarLessons.title: Plural nouns use several patterns
grammarLessons.explanation: Sinhala has several plural patterns rather than one universal ending, so learn frequent nouns together with their plurals.

examples.en: The children are at school.
There are books on the table.
People are waiting for the bus.

grammarLessons.title: Having with a dative possessor
grammarLessons.explanation: Spoken Sinhala often expresses have as something existing to a person. Use ඉන්නවා when the possessed referent is animate.

examples.en: I have a car.
He or she has a brother.
We have time today.

grammarLessons.explanation: In speech, -යි can mark each item in a coordinated list. සහ is a more formal alternative for and.

The bus went quickly.

referenceLessons.title: Everyday actions
referenceLessons.goal: Build short present-tense sentences about common activities.

grammarLessons.title: Default subject-object-verb order
grammarLessons.explanation: A neutral Sinhala sentence normally places the main verb last.

examples.en: I read the book.
I drink tea.
She writes a letter.
I drink coffee.
We listen to songs.
You make food.
He or she opens the door.
She starts the class.
They hit the ball.

grammarLessons.title: Present and regular actions with -නවා
grammarLessons.explanation: The common colloquial -නවා form covers present, habitual, and contextually future actions.

examples.en: I study Sinhala every day.
He or she drinks coffee in the morning.
We play cricket on weekends.
I drink water in the morning.
You work on Saturdays.
He or she walks in the evening.
We listen to Sinhala every day.
She cooks twice a week.
They play after school.

grammarLessons.title: Omitted subjects

I will stay here for a little while.
I am going to the shop now.
I am coming again tomorrow.
I will stay a little.
I will talk later.

I will read slowly.

referenceLessons.title: Food and drink
referenceLessons.goal: Name staple foods and ask for something to eat or drink.

grammarLessons.title: Wants and needs with ඕනේ
grammarLessons.explanation: The person who wants something often appears in the dative form.

examples.en: I want a tea.
I want a bottle of water.
We need two rooms.

grammarLessons.title: Alternatives with හරි ... හරි
grammarLessons.explanation: Repeating හරි after alternatives creates an everyday either-or choice.

examples.en: Have either tea or coffee.
Come either today or tomorrow.

examples.si: බස් එකෙන් හරි දුම්රියෙන් හරි යමු.
examples.en: Let us go either by bus or by train.

grammarLessons.title: Also and too with -ත්
grammarLessons.explanation: The particle -ත් adds the meaning also, too, or even to the item before it.

examples.en: I am coming tomorrow too.
He or she wants tea too.
We speak Sinhala too.

referenceLessons.title: Time, days, and schedules
referenceLessons.goal: Ask the time and place an event on a day or at a time.

grammarLessons.title: Time and place before the verb
grammarLessons.explanation: Time and place information usually arrives before the final action.

examples.en: I am going home today.
We are going to school tomorrow.
He or she goes to the shop in the morning.
I am going to the shop today.
We are going to the beach tomorrow.
He or she is staying home tonight.
She goes to the office in the morning.
They go to the temple in the evening.
You are going to class now.

grammarLessons.title: Ordinal numbers before nouns
grammarLessons.explanation: Ordinal forms such as first and second normally come before the noun they rank.

examples.en: This is the first lesson.
He or she took the second bus.
Today is the third day.

grammarLessons.title: Dative -ට for to, for, and experiencers
grammarLessons.explanation: The -ට ending can mark a recipient, destination, or the person who feels, needs, or experiences something.

examples.en: I need water.
She feels cold.
We do not have time.
I need more time.
Do you understand?
She is afraid.
We are free today.
He or she is happy.
They need help.

grammarLessons.title: Dative -ට for to, for, and experiencers
grammarLessons.explanation: The -ට ending can mark a recipient, destination, or the person who feels, needs, or experiences something.

examples.en: I need water.
She feels cold.
We do not have time.
I need more time.
Do you understand?
She is afraid.
We are free today.
He or she is happy.
They need help.

grammarLessons.title: From a place with -ින්
grammarLessons.explanation: The same family of endings commonly marks movement from a place.
grammarLessons.exampleEn: He or she left from home.

examples.en: He or she left from home.
I came from Colombo.
The bus left from Kandy.

grammarLessons.title: Manner words before the action
grammarLessons.explanation: Words describing how an action happens, such as slowly or well, usually appear before the final verb.

examples.en: Please speak slowly.
He or she speaks Sinhala well.
The bus went quickly.

grammarLessons.title: By or with using -න් / -ින්
grammarLessons.explanation: Instrumental forms can express the tool, means, or source involved in an event.

examples.en: I came by bus.
He or she wrote with a pencil.
We went to Kandy by train.

grammarLessons.title: Future meaning from time and context
grammarLessons.explanation: Colloquial Sinhala often uses a nonpast form with හෙට or another future time expression.

examples.en: I will come tomorrow.
We will go to Jaffna next week.
He or she will call tonight.
I will call tomorrow.
We will take a trip next month.
He or she will study tonight.
You will tell me later.
They have a meeting on Monday.
She will go home at the weekend.

referenceLessons.title: මම, මට, මාව: everyday case roles
referenceLessons.goal: Choose the natural pronoun form for a normal subject, a dative experiencer or target, and a direct object.

grammarLessons.title: Experiencers with මට, ඔයාට, and එයාට
grammarLessons.explanation: For wants, needs, ability, liking, feelings, and many bodily states, everyday Sinhala commonly marks the person with -ට. Do not automatically copy an English subject pronoun into Sinhala.
grammarLessons.exampleEn: I want or need to eat.

examples.en: I want or need to eat.
You can do this.
He or she needs help.
I like drinking hot tea.
Do you like listening to this song?
I am hungry today.
He or she feels cold.

grammarLessons.title: Recipients and destinations with -ට
grammarLessons.explanation: -ට can mark the person who receives something or the place someone moves toward. It does not make that word a direct object.

examples.en: I gave Mom a book.
I sent you a message.
I am going to the hospital.
He or she gave Mom a tea.
We are going to the shop.
I will show you the way.
He or she went home.

grammarLessons.title: Pronoun direct objects with -ව
grammarLessons.explanation: Use forms such as මාව, ඔයාව, and එයාව when a person is directly affected by an action. Keep them separate from dative forms such as මට and ඔයාට.

examples.en: He or she saw me.
I saw you.
We met him or her.
Did you see us?
He or she knows you.
I met Mom.
He or she caught the dog.

phrases.en: I want or need to eat.

grammarLessons.title: Feelings and bodily states with -ට
grammarLessons.explanation: Hunger, thirst, cold, sleepiness, and many feelings are framed as states experienced by someone.

examples.en: I am hungry.
She feels cold.
We are sleepy.

grammarLessons.title: Inability with බෑ
grammarLessons.explanation: බෑ expresses cannot, inability, or refusal in a compact spoken form.

examples.en: I cannot come today.
I cannot understand that.
We cannot stop now.

referenceLessons.title: Daily routine and sequence
referenceLessons.goal: Connect several ordinary actions into a short account.

grammarLessons.title: Chaining actions with -ලා
grammarLessons.explanation: A -ලා participle connects a completed action to the next event.

examples.en: I ate and went home.
He or she opened the door and went inside.

examples.si: මම තේ හදලා වැඩ පටන් ගත්තා.
examples.en: I made tea and started work.
I washed my hands and ate.

examples.si: එයා බෑග් එක අරගෙන පිටත් වුණා.
examples.en: He or she took the bag and left.
We closed the door and slept.

examples.si: ඇය කවුළුව ඇරලා පිට බලලා හිටියා.
examples.en: She opened the window and looked outside.
They made tea and invited us.
Read this and tell me.

grammarLessons.title: Before doing with කලින්
grammarLessons.explanation: Place කලින් after an infinitive to say before doing that action.

examples.en: Call me before you leave.
Wash your hands before eating.

examples.si: වැඩ පටන් ගන්න කලින් මේක කියවන්න.
examples.en: Read this before starting the work.

grammarLessons.title: After an event with පස්සේ
grammarLessons.explanation: පස්සේ follows an event expression to place the main event afterward.

examples.en: We left after eating.

examples.si: වැඩ ඉවර වුණාට පස්සේ මම ගෙදර ගියා.
examples.en: I went home after the work finished.

examples.si: එයා ආවට පස්සේ අපි කතා කළා.
examples.en: We talked after he or she arrived.

phrases.en: I wake up at seven in the morning.
I eat and go to work.

phrases.si: වැඩ ඉවර වුණාට පස්සේ ගෙදර එනවා.
phrases.en: I come home after work finishes.

referenceLessons.title: Past events and storytelling
referenceLessons.goal: Tell what happened and keep events in a clear order.

grammarLessons.title: Completed past events
grammarLessons.pattern: past verb form at the end
grammarLessons.explanation: Past forms vary by verb, so learn frequent forms such as ගියා, ආවා, කළා, දැක්කා, and කිව්වා as whole units.

examples.en: We went to Colombo yesterday.
She made breakfast.
I spoke to him yesterday.
I woke up early this morning.
You read well yesterday.
He or she came by bus.
We ate dinner at night.
She wrote a letter to her friend.
They arrived on time.

grammarLessons.title: Chaining actions with -ලා
grammarLessons.explanation: A -ලා participle connects a completed action to the next event.

examples.en: I ate and went home.
He or she opened the door and went inside.

examples.si: මම තේ හදලා වැඩ පටන් ගත්තා.
examples.en: I made tea and started work.
I washed my hands and ate.

examples.si: එයා බෑග් එක අරගෙන පිටත් වුණා.
examples.en: He or she took the bag and left.
We closed the door and slept.

examples.si: ඇය කවුළුව ඇරලා පිට බලලා හිටියා.
examples.en: She opened the window and looked outside.
They made tea and invited us.
Read this and tell me.

grammarLessons.title: While or when with -ද්දී
grammarLessons.explanation: The spoken ending -ද්දී places one event during another event or situation.
grammarLessons.exampleSi: මම වැඩ කරද්දී එයා කතා කළා.
grammarLessons.exampleEn: He or she called while I was working.

examples.si: මම වැඩ කරද්දී එයා කතා කළා.
examples.en: He or she called while I was working.
He or she came while we were eating.
The children ran inside while it was raining.

grammarLessons.title: Clauses that describe nouns
grammarLessons.explanation: A verb-based description comes before the noun it modifies.
grammarLessons.exampleEn: The man who came yesterday is my friend.

examples.en: The man who came yesterday is my friend.
The book that is on the table is mine.
The film that we watched yesterday is good.

referenceLessons.title: Reasons, conditions, and plans
referenceLessons.goal: Explain why something happened and what will happen under a condition.

grammarLessons.title: Reasons with නිසා
grammarLessons.explanation: The reason normally comes first, followed by නිසා and then the result.
grammarLessons.exampleEn: Because of the rain, we did not go.

examples.en: Because of the rain, we did not go.

examples.si: රථවාහන තදබදය නිසා එයා පරක්කු වුණා.
examples.en: He or she was late because of traffic.

examples.si: විදුලිය නැති නිසා වැඩ නතර වුණා.
examples.en: The work stopped because there was no electricity.

examples.si: කාලය නැති නිසා අපි ඉක්මන් කළා.
examples.en: We hurried because there was no time.

examples.si: සද්දෙ වැඩි නිසා මට අහන්න බැරි වුණා.
examples.en: I could not hear because the noise was loud.

examples.si: අද සිසිල නිසා එයා ජැකට් එක ඇන්දා.
examples.en: He or she wore a jacket because it was cool today.

examples.si: වැඩ වැඩි නිසා ඇය පරක්කු වුණා.
examples.en: She was late because there was a lot of work.

examples.si: බස් නැති නිසා ඔවුන් ඇවිදගෙන ගියා.
examples.en: They walked because there was no bus.

examples.si: ඔයා කතා කළ නිසා මට තේරුණා.
examples.en: I understood because you explained it.

grammarLessons.title: Colloquial reasons with හින්දා
grammarLessons.explanation: හින්දා is a very common conversational way to introduce the cause of a result.
grammarLessons.exampleSi: මට වැඩ තිබුණ හින්දා එන්න බැරි වුණා.
grammarLessons.exampleEn: I could not come because I had work.

examples.si: මට වැඩ තිබුණ හින්දා එන්න බැරි වුණා.
examples.en: I could not come because I had work.

examples.si: වැස්ස වැඩි හින්දා අපි ඇතුළේ හිටියා.
examples.en: We stayed inside because it was raining heavily.

examples.si: මට සනීප නැති හින්දා වැඩට ගියේ නැහැ.
examples.en: I did not go to work because I was unwell.

grammarLessons.title: Compact conditions with -ොත්
grammarLessons.explanation: The suffixed -ොත් form creates a compact if-clause.
grammarLessons.exampleEn: If it rains, let us stay home.

examples.en: If it rains, let us stay home.
If you come, let us go together.
If he or she calls, tell me.

grammarLessons.title: Formal that-clauses with බව
grammarLessons.explanation: බව packages a fact as a noun-like clause, especially in formal speech and writing; colloquial speech often prefers කියලා.
grammarLessons.exampleEn: I know that he is coming.

examples.en: I know that he is coming.

examples.en: They announced that the meeting was canceled.

grammarLessons.title: Formal obligation with යුතුයි
grammarLessons.explanation: Formal instructions and writing often use යුතුයි for should or must, where conversation may prefer ඕනේ or වෙනවා.

examples.en: You must complete this application.

grammarLessons.title: Written copula වේ
grammarLessons.explanation: Formal written Sinhala can use වේ as is or becomes, while ordinary conversation often uses no separate copula.

examples.en: This is an important point.

examples.si: කොළඹ ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ ප්‍රධාන නගරය වේ.
examples.en: Colombo is the principal city of Sri Lanka.
Education is a fundamental right.

grammarLessons.title: Written future with -නු ඇත
grammarLessons.explanation: Formal forecasts and writing may mark future time with -නු ඇත; colloquial Sinhala usually relies on a nonpast form plus context.

examples.en: He will arrive tomorrow.

examples.si: වැඩසටහන ලබන සතියේ ආරම්භ වනු ඇත.
examples.en: The program will begin next week.
The results will be released tomorrow.

grammarLessons.title: Action nouns with -ීම
grammarLessons.explanation: The ending -ීම turns an action into a noun, especially in formal writing, headings, and instructions.

grammarLessons.title: Experiencers with මට, ඔයාට, and එයාට
grammarLessons.explanation: For wants, needs, ability, liking, feelings, and many bodily states, everyday Sinhala commonly marks the person with -ට. Do not automatically copy an English subject pronoun into Sinhala.
grammarLessons.exampleEn: I want or need to eat.

examples.en: I want or need to eat.
You can do this.
He or she needs help.
I like drinking hot tea.
Do you like listening to this song?
I am hungry today.
He or she feels cold.

grammarLessons.title: Recipients and destinations with -ට
grammarLessons.explanation: -ට can mark the person who receives something or the place someone moves toward. It does not make that word a direct object.

examples.en: I gave Mom a book.
I sent you a message.
I am going to the hospital.
He or she gave Mom a tea.
We are going to the shop.
I will show you the way.
He or she went home.

grammarLessons.title: Pronoun direct objects with -ව
grammarLessons.explanation: Use forms such as මාව, ඔයාව, and එයාව when a person is directly affected by an action. Keep them separate from dative forms such as මට and ඔයාට.

examples.en: He or she saw me.
I saw you.
We met him or her.

He or she knows you.

He or she caught the dog.

grammarLessons.title: Experiencers with මට, ඔයාට, and එයාට
grammarLessons.explanation: For wants, needs, ability, liking, feelings, and many bodily states, everyday Sinhala commonly marks the person with -ට. Do not automatically copy an English subject pronoun into Sinhala.
grammarLessons.exampleEn: I want or need to eat.

examples.en: I want or need to eat.
You can do this.
He or she needs help.
I like drinking hot tea.
Do you like listening to this song?
I am hungry today.
He or she feels cold.

grammarLessons.title: Recipients and destinations with -ට
grammarLessons.explanation: -ට can mark the person who receives something or the place someone moves toward. It does not make that word a direct object.

examples.en: I gave Mom a book.
I sent you a message.
I am going to the hospital.
He or she gave Mom a tea.
We are going to the shop.
I will show you the way.
He or she went home.

grammarLessons.title: Pronoun direct objects with -ව

examples.en: He or she saw me.
I saw you.
We met him or her.
Did you see us?
He or she knows you.
I met Mom.
He or she caught the dog.

grammarLessons.title: Present and regular actions with -නවා
grammarLessons.explanation: The common colloquial -නවා form covers present, habitual, and contextually future actions.

examples.en: I study Sinhala every day.
He or she drinks coffee in the morning.
We play cricket on weekends.
I drink water in the morning.
You work on Saturdays.
He or she walks in the evening.
We listen to Sinhala every day.
She cooks twice a week.
They play after school.

grammarLessons.title: Infinitives ending in -න්න
grammarLessons.explanation: The -න්න form expresses to do and combines with wants, ability, purpose, and other verbs.

examples.en: I want to speak Sinhala.
We need to leave early.
She went to the shop to buy the book.
I want to stay a little longer.
We need to understand this.
He or she went to the shop to buy bread.
She tried to fall asleep quickly.

referenceLessons.title: Sinhala verbs 1-20
referenceLessons.goal: Study 20 Sinhala verbs, their main forms, and preserved romanized alternatives.

grammarLessons.title: Present and regular actions with -නවා
grammarLessons.explanation: The common colloquial -නවා form covers present, habitual, and contextually future actions.

examples.en: I study Sinhala every day.
He or she drinks coffee in the morning.
We play cricket on weekends.
I drink water in the morning.
You work on Saturdays.
He or she walks in the evening.
We listen to Sinhala every day.
She cooks twice a week.
They play after school.

grammarLessons.title: Completed past events
grammarLessons.pattern: past verb form at the end
grammarLessons.explanation: Past forms vary by verb, so learn frequent forms such as ගියා, ආවා, කළා, දැක්කා, and කිව්වා as whole units.

examples.en: We went to Colombo yesterday.
She made breakfast.
I spoke to him yesterday.
I woke up early this morning.
You read well yesterday.
He or she came by bus.
We ate dinner at night.
She wrote a letter to her friend.
They arrived on time.

grammarLessons.title: Infinitives ending in -න්න
grammarLessons.explanation: The -න්න form expresses to do and combines with wants, ability, purpose, and other verbs.

examples.en: I want to speak Sinhala.
We need to leave early.
She went to the shop to buy the book.
I want to stay a little longer.
We need to understand this.
He or she went to the shop to buy bread.
She tried to fall asleep quickly.

examples.si: ඔවුන් ගමන පටන් ගන්න ලෑස්ති වුණා.
examples.en: They got ready to start the trip.
Can you read this?

grammarLessons.title: Chaining actions with -ලා
grammarLessons.explanation: A -ලා participle connects a completed action to the next event.

examples.en: I ate and went home.
He or she opened the door and went inside.

examples.si: මම තේ හදලා වැඩ පටන් ගත්තා.
examples.en: I made tea and started work.
I washed my hands and ate.

examples.si: එයා බෑග් එක අරගෙන පිටත් වුණා.
examples.en: He or she took the bag and left.
We closed the door and slept.

examples.si: ඇය කවුළුව ඇරලා පිට බලලා හිටියා.
examples.en: She opened the window and looked outside.
They made tea and invited us.
Read this and tell me.

progressiveGuide.title: Simple present versus ongoing action
progressiveGuide.pattern: habitual: verb + නවා · ongoing: verb + මින් ඉන්නවා
progressiveGuide.description: The -නවා form is the regular or habitual present. Use -මින් ඉන්නවා when you want to emphasize that the action is happening right now.

examples.en: He/she eats rice every day.
He/she is eating rice now.

rules.title: Infinitive to Present / Nonpast
rules.description: Standard conversion of the infinitive form ending in -anna/inna/enna to the present or habitual nonpast -anava/inava/enava. This is not a dedicated English-style continuous form; use a -මින් ඉන්නවා construction to make an ongoing action explicit.

rules.title: Conjunctive Participle Formation
rules.description: Formation of the 'having done' or 'after doing' form, often ending in -la or -illa.
rules.note: Irregular roots like ya- (to go) change significantly to gihilla.

rules.title: Past Tense Regular Transformation
rules.description: Most past tense forms involve changing the root vowel (e.g., a - e) and appending a suffix like -uva, -a, or -una.

rules.title: Intransitive/Passive marker -enava
rules.description: Verbs ending in -enava typically indicate an involuntary action, passive state, or motion, and often take a past tense ending in -una.

forms.label: Infinitive
forms.function: Use before helpers such as ඕනේ, ආසයි, and පුළුවන්.

examples.en: I want/need to eat rice.
He/she likes to eat rice.
We are getting ready to eat rice.

forms.label: Present / nonpast
forms.function: Use for simple present, habitual, or contextually future actions; use -මින් ඉන්නවා to make an action explicitly ongoing.

examples.en: I eat rice every day.
He/she eats rice now.
We eat rice.

forms.label: Past
forms.function: Use for a completed action.

examples.en: I did eat rice yesterday.
He/she did eat rice.
We did eat rice.

forms.label: Conjunctive participle
forms.function: Use to link this action to the next one or to show it as completed.

examples.en: I have finished eating rice.
He/she went after eating rice.
He/she has completed eating rice.

progressiveGuide.title: Simple present versus ongoing action
progressiveGuide.pattern: habitual: verb + නවා · ongoing: verb + මින් ඉන්නවා
progressiveGuide.description: The -නවා form is the regular or habitual present. Use -මින් ඉන්නවා when you want to emphasize that the action is happening right now.

examples.en: He/she eats rice every day.
He/she is eating rice now.

rules.title: Infinitive to Present / Nonpast
rules.description: Standard conversion of the infinitive form ending in -anna/inna/enna to the present or habitual nonpast -anava/inava/enava. This is not a dedicated English-style continuous form; use a -මින් ඉන්නවා construction to make an ongoing action explicit.

rules.title: Conjunctive Participle Formation
rules.description: Formation of the 'having done' or 'after doing' form, often ending in -la or -illa.
rules.note: Irregular roots like ya- (to go) change significantly to gihilla.

rules.title: Past Tense Regular Transformation
rules.description: Most past tense forms involve changing the root vowel (e.g., a - e) and appending a suffix like -uva, -a, or -una.

rules.title: Intransitive/Passive marker -enava
rules.description: Verbs ending in -enava typically indicate an involuntary action, passive state, or motion, and often take a past tense ending in -una.

forms.label: Infinitive

forms.label: Present / nonpast
forms.function: Use for simple present, habitual, or contextually future actions; use -මින් ඉන්නවා to make an action explicitly ongoing.

examples.en: I learn Sinhala every day.
He/she learns Sinhala now.
We learn Sinhala.

forms.label: Past
forms.function: Use for a completed action.

examples.en: I did learn Sinhala yesterday.
He/she did learn Sinhala.
We did learn Sinhala.

forms.label: Conjunctive participle
forms.function: Use to link this action to the next one or to show it as completed.

examples.en: I have finished learning Sinhala.
He/she went after learning Sinhala.
He/she has completed learning Sinhala.

progressiveGuide.title: Simple present versus ongoing action
progressiveGuide.pattern: habitual: verb + නවා · ongoing: verb + මින් ඉන්නවා
progressiveGuide.description: The -නවා form is the regular or habitual present. Use -මින් ඉන්නවා when you want to emphasize that the action is happening right now.

examples.en: He/she eats rice every day.
He/she is eating rice now.

rules.title: Infinitive to Present / Nonpast
rules.description: Standard conversion of the infinitive form ending in -anna/inna/enna to the present or habitual nonpast -anava/inava/enava. This is not a dedicated English-style continuous form; use a -මින් ඉන්නවා construction to make an ongoing action explicit.

rules.title: Conjunctive Participle Formation
rules.description: Formation of the 'having done' or 'after doing' form, often ending in -la or -illa.
rules.note: Irregular roots like ya- (to go) change significantly to gihilla.

rules.title: Past Tense Regular Transformation
rules.description: Most past tense forms involve changing the root vowel (e.g., a - e) and appending a suffix like -uva, -a, or -una.

rules.title: Intransitive/Passive marker -enava
rules.description: Verbs ending in -enava typically indicate an involuntary action, passive state, or motion, and often take a past tense ending in -una.

grammarLessons.title: Present and regular actions with -නවා
grammarLessons.explanation: The common colloquial -නවා form covers present, habitual, and contextually future actions.

examples.en: I study Sinhala every day.
He or she drinks coffee in the morning.
We play cricket on weekends.
I drink water in the morning.
You work on Saturdays.
He or she walks in the evening.
We listen to Sinhala every day.
She cooks twice a week.
They play after school.

grammarLessons.title: Completed past events
grammarLessons.pattern: past verb form at the end
grammarLessons.explanation: Past forms vary by verb, so learn frequent forms such as ගියා, ආවා, කළා, දැක්කා, and කිව්වා as whole units.

examples.en: We went to Colombo yesterday.
She made breakfast.
I spoke to him yesterday.
I woke up early this morning.
You read well yesterday.
He or she came by bus.
We ate dinner at night.
She wrote a letter to her friend.
They arrived on time.

grammarLessons.title: Infinitives ending in -න්න
grammarLessons.explanation: The -න්න form expresses to do and combines with wants, ability, purpose, and other verbs.

examples.en: I want to speak Sinhala.
We need to leave early.
She went to the shop to buy the book.
I want to stay a little longer.
We need to understand this.
He or she went to the shop to buy bread.
She tried to fall asleep quickly.

examples.si: ඔවුන් ගමන පටන් ගන්න ලෑස්ති වුණා.
examples.en: They got ready to start the trip.
Can you read this?

grammarLessons.title: Chaining actions with -ලා
grammarLessons.explanation: A -ලා participle connects a completed action to the next event.

examples.en: I ate and went home.
He or she opened the door and went inside.

examples.si: මම තේ හදලා වැඩ පටන් ගත්තා.
examples.en: I made tea and started work.

examples.si: එයා බෑග් එක අරගෙන පිටත් වුණා.
examples.en: He or she took the bag and left.
